label: Eye test and glasses

what_happens.title: What happens at the eye test
goals: The eye doctor checks how well eyes see
You look at pictures, letters and lights
what_happens.parentSkill: Play a game at home: cover one eye and name pictures across the room.

who_is_there.title: Who checks my eyes
who_is_there.parentSkill: Point out people wearing glasses, including favourite characters and family.

what_i_do.title: What I do at the eye test
goals: Keep my head still and look where asked
Blink, look up for drops if needed
what_i_do.parentSkill: Practise "chin on the rest, look at the light" with a cup and a flashlight.

if_scared.title: If it feels strange
goals: A dark room and bright lights can feel strange
Drops can sting for a moment
Calm tools: slow breaths, a hand to hold, a break
if_scared.parentSkill: Be honest about drops: 'They may sting for a few seconds. Then they stop.'

rehearsal.title: Let's practise the eye test
goals: Play eye doctor with a picture chart
Practise looking up for drops with water
rehearsal.parentSkill: Make a picture chart, play eye doctor, and practise looking up while you pretend to give drops.

steps: Arrive at the eye doctor and check in
Sit in a big chair in a room that can go dark
Look at pictures or letters on a chart and say what I see
Look through a big machine with lenses that click
Maybe get eye drops that sting for a moment and make eyes blurry
The eye doctor shines a little light to look inside the eyes
Choose glasses frames, if glasses are needed
sensory: a dark room with a bright chart
a big machine with clicking lenses
a small bright light close to the eye
eye drops that feel cold and may sting
new glasses sitting on the nose and ears
honestyNotes: Eye drops can sting for a few seconds and can make vision blurry and eyes sensitive to light for a few hours; never promise they will feel like nothing. The test itself has no wrong answers. If glasses are needed, they may feel strange for a few days.

fallbackAnswer: Drops can feel cold and sting for a few seconds.
Then it stops, and things look blurry for a while.

questionButtons.text: What if I get the answers wrong?
fallbackAnswer: There are no wrong answers. Just say what you see.
Guessing is okay.

questionButtons.text: Why does the room go dark?
fallbackAnswer: A dark room makes the chart and the lights easier to see.
The lights come back on after.
The eye doctor will tell you. Lots of kids wear glasses.
Glasses help your eyes see clearly.
Yes, [[GROWNUP]] stays in the room.
You can hold a hand during the drops.
It has lenses that click, to find which one helps you see best.
You just look and say, one or two.
A doctor whose job is checking eyes.
They tell you each step before they do it.

questionButtons.text: Will kids tease me about glasses?
fallbackAnswer: Lots of kids wear glasses, and most kids think they look cool.
If anyone is unkind, tell a teacher and [[GROWNUP]].

questionButtons.text: Why is the light so bright?
fallbackAnswer: The little light helps the doctor see inside your eye.
You can close your eyes for a rest after.
You go home, maybe with sunglasses if you had drops.
If you need glasses, you choose frames.
Some older kids wear contacts. The eye doctor can tell you when it might be an option.
Glasses are the usual start.

techniques.label: A home eye chart
techniques.how: Make a picture chart and play eye doctor.

techniques.label: Look-up practice
techniques.how: Practise looking at the ceiling for drops.

techniques.label: Holding a hand
techniques.how: Hold your child's hand during drops.

techniques.label: Sunglasses after
techniques.how: Bring sunglasses for after the drops.

techniques.label: No wrong answers
techniques.how: Remind your child that guessing is okay.

techniques.label: Glasses heroes
techniques.how: Point out favourite people and characters who wear glasses.

techniques.label: Asking what it does
techniques.how: Encourage asking what each machine does.

techniques.label: Choosing frames
techniques.how: Let your child choose the colour and shape of frames.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

ritual: Chin still, look at the chart

pain: The drops may sting for a moment, then stop.
body: Glasses help your eyes see clearly.
Lots of eyes need a little help.
sensory: The room goes dark so the chart is easy to see.
The light is bright. You can rest your eyes after.
strangers: The eye doctor will tell you each step.
You can ask what the machine does.
separation: I'm right here in the room.
safety: You can ask for a break.
social: Your friends will think they look great.
love: I love your eyes, with or without glasses.

sentences.text: Soon [[CHILD]] will have an eye test.
An eye test checks how well the eyes can see, near and far.
First [[CHILD]] sits in a big chair in a room that can go dark.
Then a chart lights up with pictures or letters.
Before bed, here is a story about a little owl called Iris.
Iris kept bumping into branches at dusk.
Mama Owl took her to the eye doctor, a wise old heron.
First Iris sat on a big perch in a dim room.
Then a chart glowed with pictures: a leaf, a fish, a moon.
Iris said the big ones easily, but the tiny ones looked fuzzy.
Next the heron put clicking lenses in front of her eyes.
One or two, which is clearer, asked the heron.
Two, said Iris, and the leaf looked sharp.
Then the heron said, little glasses will help you see the branches.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
[[CHILD]] says what each one is, big ones first, then small ones.
Next comes a machine with lenses that click, which one is clearer, one or two?
After that, the eye doctor shines a little light to look inside the eyes.
Last, the doctor says if the eyes need any help, like glasses.
[[CHILD]] can say, I am not sure, if a picture looks blurry.

At the eye test, an eye doctor checks the eyes.
The eye doctor is called an optometrist or an ophthalmologist.
A helper may do the first part, like the chart.
[[GROWNUP]] stays in the room the whole time.
[[CHILD]] can ask the doctor, what is that machine for?
In the story, Iris the owl met the eye helpers.
Doctor Heron had kind eyes behind big round glasses.
You wear glasses too, said Iris.
I do, said the heron, they help me read.
A cheerful sparrow helped Iris choose frames.
There were red ones, blue ones, round ones and square ones.
Mama Owl sat close by and watched.
Iris tried on purple frames and looked in the mirror.
Those fit just right, said the sparrow.
Iris thought she looked very clever.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
The doctor explains each step before doing it.
Lots of kids and grown-ups wear glasses.
At the glasses shop, a helper helps choose frames.
They make sure the glasses fit just right.
[[CHILD]] can ask the doctor, what is that machine for?

In the story, Iris the owl kept her head very still.
Look at the light, said the heron, and Iris looked.
Then she looked at the little toy fish.
Is it clear or fuzzy, asked the heron.
A bit fuzzy, said Iris, honestly.
That is helpful, said the heron.
Then came eye drops.
Iris looked up at the ceiling, and drip.
It felt cold and stung for a moment, and Iris blinked and blinked.
Then it stopped, and everything looked soft and blurry for a while.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
For the machine, put the chin on the chin rest and look inside.
If eye drops are needed, look up, and blink after.
If the light feels bright, close the eyes for a rest.
At the end, choose a sticker, or glasses frames.

In the story, Iris the owl played eye doctor with Papa.
They drew a chart with a big moon and a tiny star.
Papa covered one eye and squinted.
Is that a star or a sock, he said, and Iris giggled.
Then Iris was the patient.
She looked up, and Papa pretended to drip drops, plip.
Iris blinked and blinked, like a real patient.
Then she put on paper glasses and hooted at the mirror.
Papa said, you know all the steps.
Iris felt ready.
And Iris slept well that night.
After that, they practise looking up at the ceiling for pretend drops, and blinking.
Last, [[CHILD]] tries on pretend glasses and looks in the mirror.
Practising makes the real visit feel easy.

Eye doctors measure sharpness of vision, how the eyes focus, and how they work together.
Being near-sighted means far things look blurry, and far-sighted means close things are harder.
The clicking lenses find the exact strength that makes things clear.
Many kids do not notice blurry vision because they think everyone sees that way.
[[CHILD]] can ask the doctor to show what their eyes look like on the screen.
Optometrists do eye tests and prescribe glasses; ophthalmologists are medical doctors who also treat eye diseases.
Opticians fit the glasses so they sit at the right height.
About one in four school kids needs glasses at some point.
Many athletes, scientists and actors wear glasses or contact lenses.
[[CHILD]] can choose frames that match their style.
Honest answers give the most accurate result, so guessing to sound good does not help.
Dilating drops widen the pupil so the doctor can see the back of the eye, and the effect lasts a few hours.
Sunglasses help after drops because light feels brighter.
The machine that puffs air or flashes is checking pressure and shape, and it is quick.
[[CHILD]] can ask the doctor to explain the result in simple words.
Feeling uneasy with things near your eyes is a natural reflex that protects them.
Keeping both eyes closed briefly after drops helps them spread and reduces stinging.
Blurry near vision after dilation means reading or screens are hard for a few hours.
If glasses are needed, getting used to them takes a few days, and headaches at first are common.
[[CHILD]] can plan a relaxing activity, like an audiobook, for after the drops.
Knowing that the test is about finding the right lens, not passing or failing, takes the pressure off.
Writing down any problems noticed, like headaches or squinting at the board, helps the doctor.
Bringing sunglasses makes the trip home comfortable after drops.
If glasses are prescribed, choosing frames is a chance to show personality.
[[CHILD]] can make a list of frame colours to look for.
